newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: FORECAST-Irish inflation pressure to remain modest.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Irish inflation pressure to remain modest.

text.p: Irish inflation data this week is expected to show consumer price pressure remained moderate in April and the outlook for this year looks benign despite the Irish pound's recent woes, analysts said on Tuesday.
Experts predict Thursday's figures will show a monthly rise of between 0.1 percent and 0.3 percent after a 0.1 percent rise in March.

The Irish pound's recent sharp drop against sterling is only likely to make itself felt towards the end of the year. Seasonal food price pressure appears to have remained modest while oil and petrol prices have dropped, helping cap the CPI, they said.
Estimates for annual inflation range between 1.3 and 1.6 percent although analysts warned predictions have been complicated because monthly records have only been available from this year.

"We have no previous data to go on so it's all something of a shot in the dark. We've pencilled in 0.2 percent for the month and an annualised increase of 1.5 percent," Michael Crowley, economist at Davy stockbrokers, said.
"As of now, inflation looks fairly subdued and it seems likely that we will meet the Maastricht inflation criteria for this year. There are no particular concerns in the index components," he added.
Eunan King, economist at NCB stockbrokers, echoed Crowley's caution on reading too much into the figures and also his optimism for this year's trend despite the Irish pound's recent battering.

"We're going for 0.2 percent on the month and 1.4 percent for the year. We haven't got a lot of information on this and are just being a bit cautious. We're not placing too much significance on 0.2 versus 0.1," he said.

"We just think we will continue with fairly modest inflation for the next few months...Inflation isn't going to rise anywhere near the (Maastricht) limit, which is 2.6 percent at the minute. Even if you had a big pick-up in inflation late this year or early next year (because of the pound's fall), it probably wouldn't even put us above two percent," he said.
Analysts said the Irish pound's recent drop against sterling would only feed through in inflation possibly toward the end of the year or in early 1998.
The Irish currency was hammered last week, hitting a five-year low against sterling, after Ireland's central bank indicated it would not act to shore up the currency.
"Now it's about 1.5 percent below last year. We think that will add something to inflation but not enough to bring us above about two percent year on year in March 1998," King said.

For the European Union harmonised index of consumer prices (HICP), which is used for intra-EU comparisons, Bloxham Stockbrokers predicts a monthly rise of 0.1 percent in April and a yearly rise of 0.9 percent.
The HICP for March showed no change and was up 1.7 percent for the 13 months from February last year.
The Central Statistics Office is expected to release the CPI data at 1100 GMT on Thursday.
